deep.reconstruction:
The page holds four separate notebook entries, divided by horizontal rules. Two are mathematical and two are methodological or personal maxims.

(1) Programme for algebraic functions. One can derive the theory of algebraic functions of one variable while avoiding Cramer's rule, which is only the formal execution. The derivation would use only the Riemann surface (its cycles, i.e. its topology/homology) and the elementary theorems on power series. No derivation is given.

In modern terms: let F(x,y)=0 be irreducible and let X be its compact Riemann surface. The plan is to build the field C(X), with its divisors, Abelian integrals and periods over the cycles of X, from two ingredients only:
- local Puiseux or power-series uniformisation;
- the topology of X.

It would not use the determinant and elimination machinery. That machinery appears in Kronecker-style or Weierstrass/Brill-Noether-style treatments, e.g. in solving linear systems for the coefficients of adjoint polynomials. This is a methodological remark, not a computation.

(2) Maxim. Everything one has ever learned should be regarded as prejudice and doubted. It becomes reliable only after one has thought it through exactly oneself. Until then it should carry a cross (= Kritik!), meaning 'caution!' or 'reservation!'. There is no mathematics here.

(3) Maxim on genius. The phrase 'he is a genius' is only an embarrassed phrase by which laziness tries to whitewash itself. We have no idea how industrious Goethe, Lessing and Gauss were. Nothing is achieved without effort. Genius and talent are properties of character, will and energy. There is no mathematics here.

(4) Galois group and multiple roots. The theorem that every equation has a group holds in general only for equations whose discriminant is nonzero. Example: (x^2-2)^2 = 0 has no group.

Reconstruction (mine): (x^2-2)^2 = x^4 - 4x^2 + 4 has roots x1=x2=sqrt2 and x3=x4=-sqrt2. Its discriminant is 0. Galois's construction of the group of an equation needs pairwise distinct roots, for two reasons:
- It uses a Lagrange/Galois resolvent V = sum c_i x_i that takes n! distinct values under the permutations of the roots. This is impossible when x1=x2.
- Galois's characterisation is that the group is the set of permutations σ such that a rational function φ(x1..xn) is rationally known iff φ is formally invariant under σ. This fails here. The function x1 - x2 is not formally invariant under (13), yet it has the known value 0. Conversely, x1 is not formally invariant under (12), yet (12) preserves every numerical relation.

So the permutation group 'of the equation' is not well defined as a group of permutations of its n roots. One must first pass to the squarefree part x^2 - 2, which has discriminant 8 ≠ 0 and Galois group C2. The 'im Allgemeinen' (inserted above the line) acknowledges that the condition D ≠ 0 is sufficient in the classical setting.
errors: No mathematical error. 'keine Gruppe' is correct only in the classical sense: a permutation group on the n roots counted with multiplicity, defined via Galois resolvents. In modern terms the splitting field Q(sqrt2) still has Galois group C2, which is the group of the squarefree part x^2-2.
The Riemann-surface programme in entry (1) is only asserted, not carried out. Avoiding linear algebra entirely is optimistic: Riemann-Roch-type dimension counts still involve linear systems.

results.what: Theory of algebraic functions of one variable to be founded purely on the Riemann surface (cycles/topology) plus local power-series theory, avoiding determinantal/elimination formalism
results.modern_name: Transcendental/topological foundation of the theory of algebraic functions (compact Riemann surfaces, function fields via uniformisation)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857) for the idea; systematic rigorous form by Hermann Weyl, 'Die Idee der Riemannschen Fläche' (1913), with Dirichlet-principle foundations via Hilbert (1900-04)

results.what: Galois group (as permutation group of the roots) is defined only for equations with nonzero discriminant; example (x^2-2)^2=0
results.modern_name: Separability/squarefreeness hypothesis in classical Galois theory
results.usually_credited_to: Galois (1831 memoir assumes no equal roots); standard in Jordan (1870), Weber's Lehrbuch

deep.surprise_reason: The Galois remark is a standard caveat. The Riemann-surface programme is a known Göttingen-style viewpoint that Weyl later realised. The maxims are interesting biographically, reflecting Hilbert's views on work and genius, but are not mathematical novelties.

checkable.asserts: The example equation has vanishing discriminant (multiple roots).
Expanded form of the example equation.
The squarefree part, to which the group should properly be attached, is x^2-2.
The squarefree part has nonzero discriminant, so its Galois group (C2) is defined classically.
